chapters.name: Chapter 1: Choosing your certificate and planning to finish

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What data analysts and data scientists do
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Describe the data workflow and say which part interests you most.
This lesson builds toward: Given a workplace you know, you will describe the data workflow and write three questions data could answer there, marking each one as analyst or data scientist work.
Data work follows a simple path: ask a question, collect the data, clean it, explore and analyze it, show it with charts, and share what it means. Google's program describes the same idea in its own steps.
A data analyst mostly works with what already happened: "Which product sold best last month?" They use spreadsheets, SQL (a language for asking questions of databases) and dashboard tools like Tableau or Power BI.
A data scientist does that too, and also builds models that predict or sort things: "Which customers might stop buying?" They usually code in Python and use more math. Many people start as analysts and grow into data science.
Words to know:
- Data set: a collection of data, usually a table of rows and columns.
- SQL: Structured Query Language: a language for getting data out of databases.
- Model: a program that learns patterns from data to predict or sort things.
- Dashboard: a page of charts that updates as the data changes.
Try it now: Think of your current or last job (a store, warehouse, clinic, restaurant). Write three questions data could answer there, such as "Which hours are busiest?" Mark each one "analyst" or "data scientist".
You can now describe the data workflow and the difference between a data analyst and a data scientist.

check.q: What is the usual first step of the data workflow?
check.why: Data work starts with a clear question, which guides every later step.

check.q: At your store you want to know which hours are busiest. Whose kind of work is that?
check.why: Describing what happened, such as busy hours, is typical analyst work.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Comparing the well-known data certificates
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Compare three widely known data certificates and pick the one that fits your goal.
This lesson builds toward: Given three well-known data certificates, you will compare their level, main tools, time and cost and choose the one that fits your goal, with the cost taken from the official page today.
Google Data Analytics Professional Certificate (on Coursera): a 9-course series for beginners, no experience needed. Its page lists spreadsheets, SQL, Tableau and presentations, and its FAQ says it teaches Python. It suggests about 6 months at 10 hours a week.
IBM Data Science Professional Certificate (on Coursera): a 12-course series for beginners. Its page lists Python, SQL, Jupyter and libraries like Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib and Scikit-learn, and covers data analysis, visualization and machine learning models. It suggests about 4 months at 10 hours a week.
Microsoft Certified: Power BI Data Analyst Associate: an intermediate certification earned by passing Exam PL-300, a proctored exam. It tests preparing, modeling, visualizing and analyzing data in Power BI, and you renew it every 12 months for free on Microsoft Learn.
Costs, times and course lists change, and some programs are included in subscriptions or offered free through libraries, workforce boards or financial aid. Open each official page and check before you enroll. No certificate guarantees a job.
Step by step:
- Write your goal: analyst, data scientist, or using data in your current job.
- Open each certificate's official page.
- Write down its level, tools, length and current cost.
- Ask your local workforce center or library about free access.
- Choose one, and write why.
Words to know:
- Professional certificate: a series of online courses from a company or school that ends with a certificate.
- Proctored exam: a test watched by an official, in person or online, to prevent cheating.
- Python: a popular programming language used in data science.
Official sources:
- Coursera: Google Data Analytics Professional Certificate
- Coursera: IBM Data Science Professional Certificate
- Microsoft Learn: Microsoft Certified: Power BI Data Analyst Associate (Exam PL-300)
Try it now: Make a three-row comparison table: certificate, level, main tools, time, cost today (from the official page). Circle the one that fits your goal and write one sentence saying why.
You can now compare the Google, IBM and Microsoft data certificates and choose one that fits your goal.

check.q: What does earning a data certificate guarantee?
options: Nothing; it shows what you learned
check.why: A certificate shows skills; it does not guarantee a job.

check.q: A friend says a certificate costs a certain amount a month. What do you do before enrolling?
options: Ask an AI for the price
Check the cost on the program's official page today
check.why: Costs change, so you check the official page at the time you enroll.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Making a study plan you will keep
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a weekly study plan that fits around work and family.
This lesson builds toward: For the certificate you chose, you will create a weekly study plan with set study blocks and a weekly goal, that fits around your work and family.
Most people who do not finish a certificate stop because life gets busy, not because it was too hard. A plan written down, with set times, makes finishing much more likely.
Start with your real week. If you work shifts, pick study blocks that fit: for example, three 45-minute blocks on weekdays and one 2-hour block on the weekend. Short, regular study beats one long weekend session.
Each week, set one small goal you can check off: "finish module 2 and its quiz". Keep notes in your own words, and do every hands-on lab: the labs are where the skill is built. An AI assistant can explain a confusing idea in simpler words or quiz you, but do the graded work yourself and follow the program's honesty rules.
Step by step:
- Write down your fixed hours: work, family, sleep.
- Pick 3-5 study blocks a week and put them in your calendar.
- Set one weekly goal you can check off.
- Ask a friend or AI assistant to quiz you on your notes.
- Review every Sunday and adjust.
Words to know:
- Study block: a set time in your calendar for learning.
- Lab: a hands-on exercise where you practice a skill on real data or code.
Try it now: Put four study blocks for next week into your phone or paper calendar. Write one weekly goal from the certificate you chose, for example "finish the first module".
You can now make a weekly study plan with set times and a goal you can check off.

check.q: Where is the real skill built in an online course?
check.why: Practice in the labs builds the skill employers want to see.

check.q: You work evening shifts. Which study plan do you write?
options: Set study blocks in your calendar that fit your shifts, with a weekly goal
Study whenever you have a free day
Study eight hours in one night each month
check.why: Regular blocks in your calendar with a goal are the plan most likely to work.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Cleaning a data set
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Find and fix blanks, duplicates and format problems in a small data set.
This lesson builds toward: Given a small data set with problems, you will find and fix blanks, duplicates and format problems and write a cleaning log, with a copy of the original saved first.
Real data is messy. Before you analyze, you clean it. Every certificate above spends time on this, because wrong data gives wrong answers.
Common problems: blank cells, the same row twice (duplicates), the same thing written different ways ("CA", "Calif.", "California"), numbers stored as text, and dates in mixed formats.
In Google Sheets or Excel you can sort and filter to find problems, use Remove duplicates, use Find and replace to make names match, and change a column's format to number or date. Keep a copy of the original and write down each change you made, so others can trust your work.
Step by step:
- Save a copy of the original data.
- Sort and filter each column to spot blanks and odd values.
- Remove duplicate rows.
- Make spellings match with Find and replace.
- Set number and date formats.
- Write a short log of every change.
Words to know:
- Data cleaning: fixing errors in data before you analyze it.
- Duplicate: a row that appears more than once.
- Cleaning log: a list of every change you made to the data.
Try it now: Make a small table of 15 sales: Date, Item, Store, Amount. Put in 2 duplicate rows, one blank amount and two spellings of one store. Then clean it and write your cleaning log.
You can now find and fix common data problems and keep a cleaning log.

check.q: What is a duplicate in a data set?
options: A row that appears more than once
check.why: Duplicates count the same thing twice and make totals wrong.

check.q: You are about to clean a sales table. What do you do first?
options: Save a copy of the original
check.why: Saving the original lets you check or undo your cleaning.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Summarizing data and making one clear chart
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Answer a question with a summary table and one chart.
This lesson builds toward: Given a cleaned data set and a question, you will make a summary table and one chart that answers the question, with the right chart type and a title that states the answer.
Start with one clear question, such as "Which store sold the most last month?" A good question decides which columns you need.
A summary table groups and totals the data. In Sheets or Excel, a pivot table does this: put Store in rows and the sum of Amount in values. In Python, the Pandas library does the same with groupby. You can try Python free in Google Colab, which the IBM program's tools are similar to.
Then pick the chart that fits: a bar chart to compare groups, a line chart for change over time, and avoid pie charts with many slices. Give it a title that states the answer, like "Eastside sold the most in March", and label the axes.
Step by step:
- Write one question.
- Make a pivot table (or a Pandas groupby).
- Choose the chart: bar to compare, line for time.
- Write a title that states the answer.
- Label the axes.
Words to know:
- Pivot table: a spreadsheet tool that groups and totals data.
- Pandas: a Python library for working with tables of data.
- Bar chart: a chart that compares groups with bars of different lengths.
Official sources:
- Google Colab
Try it now: Use your cleaned table from Lesson 4. Make a pivot table of total Amount by Store, then a bar chart with a title that states the answer.
You can now turn a question into a summary table and a clear chart.

check.q: What does a pivot table do?
check.why: A pivot table groups rows, such as by store, and totals them.

check.q: You want to compare total sales across 5 stores. Which chart do you make?
options: A bar chart with a title that states the answer
check.why: Bar charts compare categories, and a title that states the answer makes it clear.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Telling the story and building a portfolio project
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short finding and package your work as a portfolio project.
This lesson builds toward: Using your chart and summary, you will write a three-sentence finding with one limit and save it as a portfolio project, with a short title and description and no private data.
Employers want to see that you can explain data, not just make charts. A good finding is three sentences: what you found, why it matters, and one limit of the data. Example: "Eastside sold 40% of March sales. It may need more staff on Saturdays. The data covers only one month."
Most of these certificates end with a capstone or portfolio project. You can start one now: a title, the question, where the data came from, your cleaning log, the chart and your finding. Use free public data, like a city open-data site, or your practice table. Never use private customer or company data without permission.
An AI assistant can help you check your writing for clarity, but make sure every number in your finding comes from your own table.
Step by step:
- Write your finding in three sentences: result, why it matters, one limit.
- Collect title, question, data source, cleaning log, chart.
- Check every number against your table.
- Save it in one place you can share, like a Google Drive folder or GitHub.
Words to know:
- Capstone: a final project at the end of a program.
- Portfolio: a collection of your work that you show employers.
- Limitation: something about the data that means the answer may not be complete.
Try it now: Final task: finish your mini portfolio project. Question, cleaned data, cleaning log, summary table, one chart and a three-sentence finding with one limit. Save it with a title and short description.
You can now complete and explain a small data project of the kind data certificates ask for.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear question No question, or one the data cannot answer. One clear question the data set can answer. The question matters to a real workplace and says why. Cleaned data and log Blanks, duplicates or format problems remain, or no log. Blanks, duplicates and formats fixed, with a cleaning log and the original saved. The log says how many rows each fix changed. Summary and chart No summary table, or a chart that does not answer the question. A summary table and one chart of the right type with a title that states the answer. Axes are labeled and the chart is easy to read at a glance. Finding and limit No finding, or no limit stated. A three-sentence finding with one limit of the data. The finding suggests a practical next step. Portfolio-ready Not saved, or contains private data. Saved in Google Sheets, Excel or Google Colab with a short title and description, and no private data. Shared as a link the learner can add to a résumé or profile. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why include one limit in your finding?
options: It shows honesty about what the data can and cannot say
check.why: Stating a limit, like covering only one month, builds trust in your work.

check.q: You want to use your employer's customer list in your public portfolio. What do you do?
options: Use a public or sample data set instead, unless you have permission
check.why: Private customer data does not go in a public portfolio without permission.
